newsitem.title: USA: Republican leader derides Clinton budget "gimmicks".
newsitem.headline: Republican leader derides Clinton budget "gimmicks".

text.p: The second ranking Republican in the Senate urged President Clinton Saturday to work with Congress on balancing the federal budget without using gimmicks or playing politics.

"We have an historic opportunity, by working together, to do some positive things to benefit American families," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles of Oklahoma said in the Republican response to Clinton's weekly radio address.
"Let us be honest with the American people, not use any gimmicks or play politics," he said.
"For example, together we can and we should balance the budget in five years," he said. "We can give tax relief to hard working Americans families. We can and we must save Medicare from bankruptcy."
"The president submitted his budget this week, and frankly we find it lacks what it takes to achieve these common goals," Nickles said.
"Is the president's plan to create new spending programmes consistent with balancing the budget? Does this administration really believe the era of big government is over?
Nickles said he did not think the budget would be balanced by the year 2002 using the figures Clinton gave. And he said Clinton's plan to save Medicare used accounting gimmicks.
His criticism echoed that of Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott Friday, who said he was disappointed by Clinton's budget plan announced Thursday.
"This is a disappointment," Lott, a Mississippi Republican, told reporters. "So much of this budget is recooked from last year."

Nickles said Republicans, who control both the Senate and House, believed there should be automatic spending cuts in government programmes if deficit targets are not reached, not automatic tax increases as proposed by Clinton.
He also called for passage of a constitutional amendment opposed by Clinton to require a balanced budget every year. Votes are expected on the amendment later this month and the outcome is in doubt.
"Yes, there are big differences in our proposals, but it is time to go to work and accomplish our common objectives," Nickles said.
"Frankly, President Clinton cannot succeed without Congress and Congress cannot succeed without the president," he said. "We must work together. The real beneficiaries will be the American people."
Clinton was scheduled to meet with Republican and Democratic congressional leaders Tuesday at the Capitol to discuss the budget and other issues.
